In brief

"Begob he drew his hand and made a swipe and let fly": all that flies off the Citizen's hand is an empty biscuitbox, but it stands in for the enormous hunk of rock that Polyphemus hurls at Odysseus in book 9 of the Odyssey. Many elements of Homer's scene find their way into Joyce's: a small weak man taunting a large strong one, companions begging the taunter to shut his mouth, a vessel struggling to get away from danger, projectiles being launched with awesome force, and combatants invoking the justice of rival gods.

At more length

After escaping from the cave and getting back to his ship, Odysseus taunts the blinded monster: "Hey, you, Cyclops! Idiot!... You had no shame at eating your own guests! / So Zeus and other gods have paid you back" (475-79, trans. Wilson). Enraged, Polyphemus "ripped / a rock out of the hill and hurled it at us. / It landed right in front of our dark prow," pushing the ship back toward shore (480-82). The crew struggle to row away and they implore their lord not to anger the giant any further: "He throws so hard!" (499). But Odysseus cannot control his fury and yells out once more, telling the giant his name. Polyphemus has heard this name: a soothsayer once told him that Odysseus would cost him his sight. "I always thought  / a tall and handsome man would visit me, endowed with strength and courage. But this weakling, / this little nobody, has blinded me; / by wine he got the best of me" (512-16). He calls on Poseidon to avenge his injury and hurls a second rock, bigger than the first, "with immeasurable force" (539).

Joyce gives his antagonist only one biscuit tin to throw but recreates other details of this scene with remarkable fidelity. His narrator echoes the comments about the giant's phenomenal arm strength: "Gob, he near sent it into the county Longford." Bloom stands on the jaunting car taunting the Citizen while his companions try to convince him to stop: "and Jack Power trying to get him to sit down on the car and hold his bloody jaw." The car is headed in the wrong direction but manages to power out of harm's way: "But as luck would have it the jarvey got the nag's head round the other way and off with him. […]  The jarvey saved his life by furious driving as sure as God made Moses." Finally, the invocations of Zeus and Poseidon are updated as a religious war between Jews and Christians, with Bloom yelling that "the Saviour was a jew" and the Citizen reciprocating: "— By Jesus, says he, I'll brain that bloody jewman for using the holy name. By Jesus, I'll crucify him so I will."

Substituting a biscuitbox for a boulder is certainly mock-heroic, but Joyce here comes as close as anywhere in Ulysses to claiming an exact resemblance between the great Odysseus and the humble Bloom.

John Hunt 2026
